name: Lena Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I give beginner drum lessons on Tuesdays, practise the percussion book for Friday community hall dances and record small parts when someone asks. I left school after secondary school and came into paid music late, so I still check my counting with the senior player.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps you at it, and what is hardest?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like watching a child keep a beat for the first time. The hard part is sending the mortgage payment while my partner’s warehouse hours and my hall dates both move around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the other players that a quicker booking form is fine, but somebody still has to play the community hall dances. I am learning the percussion parts and need the paid nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage is due even when there is no dance. My partner’s warehouse shifts change each week, and we have less than a month of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the Tuesday beginner drum pupils and the Friday hall jobs this winter. I would phone the hall manager about December dates before buying anything for the kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious already. A calm story about AI does not make our winter heating bill smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a December hall fee pay for at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The December hall fee buys the children’s winter coats. If the dance is cancelled, I would use last year’s coats and ask my partner to see whether an extra warehouse shift is open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is hard about being newer to paid music at 43?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have only secondary school behind me and started paid music late. I am not too proud to practise a simple part until it sits right.

I would keep asking for **paid hall nights**.

feel: I feel **anxious** because winter bills already press on us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the hall may use software to book acts, make posters and order backing tracks. I would ask the manager how many paid percussion dates remain before guessing what it means for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The little recording parts I play could go first, and some halls might hire fewer live players. My partner’s shift pay is not steady enough to carry the mortgage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would bring my last six hall invoices to the manager and ask for the spring booking list. If dates fall in the first year, I would cut our family takeaway nights and ask the school about an extra beginner drum class only if it pays for preparation time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed if the hall dates shrink. I already count those fees for groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which spending would you cut first and by how much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We buy takeaway twice a month, about 30 each time. I would cut both nights first and cook at home, not miss the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you take a bigger class without help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know how to teach a bigger class yet. I would ask the school’s senior tutor to watch me teach one group before I agree to take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the hall that AGI by 2028 could make scores and bookings cheaply, but a dance still needs players. I would ask for the next season’s paid dates in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My small recording work would probably go in 2028, and the hall might cancel a percussion place even before stage robots arrive around 2031. We cannot cover the mortgage for long if both that fee and a warehouse shift vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I would ask the manager for a written spring schedule and ask my partner to check stable warehouse shifts. If 2028 AGI removes my hall dates, I would apply for an open school support job and ask the mortgage lender about a temporary payment plan before we miss one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed, because I expect at least one income stream to fall and there are few music jobs nearby. I can make calls, but I cannot grow savings out of an empty calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a real school job you could apply for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school support post pays a steady weekly wage if it is open. I would apply only if it is genuinely hiring, because I cannot quit lessons for a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children and your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children we may keep the old coats another year. I would tell my partner the mortgage number plainly, not hide it behind a hopeful concert date.

say: I would ask for **written paid dates** before the next hall season.
I would tell players that a **live dance** still needs people.
think: My **recording income** may end in 2028 before hands-on robots around 2031.

do: Ask the **hall manager** for a written spring schedule tomorrow.
Apply for an **open school support post** if 2028 AGI removes hall dates.
Ask the **mortgage lender** for a temporary plan before missing a payment.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because the household expects lost income and has little saved.
S2.quote: I cannot grow savings out of an empty calendar.
fieldNote: She expects **recording loss** at 2028 AGI and hall risk before the 2031 robot arrival.
Her school application needs a **real vacancy**, while mortgage help is sought before arrears.

steps.text: Apply for an open school support job if 2028 AGI ends hall dates

Keep drum lessons while waiting for written hall dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the hall that AGI by 2031 gives us a few years to show what a live percussionist adds. I would ask for a paid apprenticeship with the senior player rather than pretend I can lead a group tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The recording parts still go by 2031 in my mind, but I might be ready to teach better by then. Stage robots around 2034 could take more dances; I do not know if people would want a robot at a family party.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This term I would ask the school’s senior tutor for one paid observation each month if the school funds it. If I can handle a group after six months, I would seek a paid beginner class; in the first year after 2031 I would keep the class only while pupils pay and the room is available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious. Four or five years is useful. The mortgage does not wait for a teaching certificate I do not have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for training before a school offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the tutor to stop me if I lose the children’s attention. I would not pay for a course before I know the school can offer paid teaching hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your family move to cut costs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children will still need shoes and school supplies each year. My partner and I would keep the current house unless we cannot make the mortgage even with steadier shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children that AGI by 2036 gives us time to learn new ways to earn, and I would still play if people hire me. I would ask the school about a real paid teaching route rather than buy gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I might teach well enough to replace some hall fees. Robots around 2039 may take stage work, but our mortgage is the thing I have to cover long before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this year I would keep a simple envelope for spare lesson fees after food and mortgage are paid. In the first year after 2036 I would compare paid teaching hours with hall income and apply for a school support post if both shrink and a vacancy exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still feel anxious because the household has almost no cushion now. Ten years gives me a training path, not a free winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you save from lessons every month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot promise money for that envelope every month. If my partner’s hours fall, we would use any extra lesson fee for groceries first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you advise your children to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children to learn a trade and also learn music if they love it. I would not make their school choice out of my fear alone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because recording fees and hall dates could fall before I can teach a full class. Written bookings, a real school vacancy and mortgage help before a missed payment would give us room.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what children hear when a parent says the band is doing fine. My children know when I count the grocery money twice.

headlineQuote: My children know when I count the grocery money twice.
portrait: At **43**, Lena is a junior percussionist and beginner teacher with secondary school education, two children and a mortgage.
Her **thin savings** and her partner’s variable warehouse shifts make even AI Plateau anxious.
She avoids **AI tools**, asks a senior tutor for funded observation and seeks paid classes only when ready.
Faster AGI risks **recording and hall fees** before she can build steadier teaching or school support work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut recording and hall fees before Lena can teach a larger paid class.
whatWouldHelp: **Written bookings**, a real school opening and early mortgage help would give the household time.
